title: Every big city should copy New York's congestion charge

defects.quote: Number plates are read at 210 detection points around the zone
defects.correction: New York's congestion pricing zone has 110 detection points, carrying more than 1,400 scanners.
defects.note: [needs-source] [multi-part] The scanner count in the same sentence (more than 1,400) is true; only the number of detection points is wrong. True value: 110. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congestion_pricing_in_New_York_City (Equipment)

defects.quote: reported 23% fewer vehicles entering the zone than a year earlier
defects.correction: In March 2025 the MTA reported a 13% decrease in vehicles entering the congestion zone compared with March 2024.

defects.quote: an estimated 17 million fewer vehicle entries
defects.correction: The MTA estimated 27 million fewer vehicle entries into the zone in the first year, a fall of about 11%.
defects.note: [needs-source] True value: 27 million. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congestion_pricing_in_New_York_City ; also reported at https://www.amny.com/news/congestion-pricing-27-million-fewer-vehicles

defects.quote: The toll brought in $38.6 million in its first month
defects.correction: The congestion toll raised $48.6 million in its first month (5 to 31 January 2025), and about $52 million in February.
defects.note: [needs-source] [multi-part] The second half of the sentence (the $230 million bond sale in October 2025) is true; only the first-month revenue is wrong. True value: $48.6 million. Source: https://www.6sqft.com/congestion-pricing-raised-48-6m-in-first-month-mta-says/ ; also https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congestion_pricing_in_New_York_City

defects.quote: On 13 March 2026 a federal judge ruled that the revocation was unlawful
defects.correction: Judge Lewis Liman ruled on 3 March 2026 that the federal revocation of approval for congestion pricing was unlawful.

defects.quote: Shops inside the zone have seen their takings rise by 30% since the toll began.
New York's traffic fell after the toll came in, so the same charge would work in every city in the world.
defects.known_rebuttal: Manhattan is an unusual case: most people who travel into the zone already do so by subway, bus or commuter rail, so drivers had an alternative to switch to and the toll had somewhere to send them. In car-dependent cities with thin public transport, such as Houston or Atlanta, a charge would mostly raise the cost of trips that people cannot avoid, which makes it both less effective and more regressive. London, Stockholm and Singapore, the usual success stories, also had dense transit before they began charging. The evidence supports congestion charging where alternatives exist, not everywhere.
